label: Part 2
title: Stress-test your plan
promise: A plan that only works on good days is not ready yet.
intro_title: Why we look at the difficult days
intro: Imagining the good day is easy. The difficult day is where the information is. Winter, illness, a quiet week with nobody around, work that goes wrong: those days happen in every life, in every country. The question is not whether they come. It is whether you could manage them in the life you are building.

finish.title: My Risks
finish.description: Your biggest risks, the signs to watch, and what you will do.

exercises.title: Two futures
intro: An option you cannot imagine on a bad day is an option you have not really considered. So you picture both: an ordinary good day and an ordinary difficult day, five years from now.

start_here.prompt: Take the option you are deciding on and, if you have one, your best alternative, such as staying and changing something. Imagine it is five years from now. For each option, write a normal good day and a normal difficult day.

fields.label: Option 1, a good day
Option 1, a difficult day
Option 2, a good day
Option 2, a difficult day

exercises.intro_after: In each day, notice who decides your time. Are your days busy by your own choice, or busy because others decide? And when do the busy transition years end: the paperwork, the renovation, finding work? More control over your time often comes after them, not straight away.

go_deeper.prompt: What would still be difficult, even after moving? Some things change with a place. Some things come with you.

story.text: After four years in Bali, the island no longer felt the same. Then I had an accident with my motorbike. It was not my fault, but I was blamed for it. It made me realise that, after all those years, I was still seen as a foreigner. When I found the self-sufficient life I wanted on YouTube, I saw two futures: staying in a place that no longer felt like home, or starting again somewhere that fitted my new picture. The hardest part was leaving the life and the friends I had built over four years, knowing I had to start again. But I knew it was the right decision.

exercises.title: What could go wrong?
intro: Fear is normal. Writing a fear down turns it into something you can work with. A fear in your head has no size. It is simply there, usually at three in the morning, and it makes every option feel dangerous. On paper, a fear gets four parts, and each part gives you something to do.

rows: Low, medium or high, or not sure. Some fears are real risks. Others are very unlikely, and naming that is a relief.
Would it cost you a weekend, or your savings? Small and likely is annoying. Big and likely needs a plan. If the impact would be serious, prepare a fallback even when you think it is unlikely.
What would you notice first, while there is still time to act? This is the most useful column.
Prevent it, reduce it, or prepare a fallback. Many fears shrink once you have one.

start_here.prompt: Check the risks of the option you are deciding on, and of your best alternative. Otherwise, you end up comparing one option's difficulties with the other option's best case.

go_deeper.prompt: Look at your biggest fear. What is it telling you? Maybe you need more information. Maybe two of your needs pull in different directions. Maybe it is a real risk to plan for.

example.text: Fear: my bakery fails in the first year. Likely: medium. Impact: big; I would lose savings. Warning sign: after six months, less than half the sales I need. What I can do: first sell at a local market for six months, set aside six months of costs, and know I can work for a bakery again.

label: Part 3
title: Put things in the right order
promise: Easy to undo first. Hard to undo last.
intro: The most expensive mistakes in a move are often not wrong choices. They are right choices made in the wrong order: selling the house before the papers are clear, signing a contract before the money is in place, or arriving before there is somewhere to live.

Do the steps you can undo cheaply first: a tax number, a bank account, a conversation with an adviser, renting, a trial period. Do the steps that are expensive or impossible to undo last: selling your home, resigning from your job, signing a purchase contract. And before each big step, write down what must be true first.
route_title: Put things in the right order

finish.title: My First Timeline
finish.description: The right steps, in the right order.

exercises.title: The right steps, in the right order

start_here.prompt: Some dates are not yours to choose, and they often decide the order. Write them down first.

row_labels: End of my rental contract, or mortgage terms
Sale or rental of my home
Visa validity (other passports: a Portuguese residency visa is valid for four months, in which you apply for your residence permit)

fields.hint: List the main steps of your move. For each one, write whether it is easy or hard to undo, what must be true first, and roughly when you would take it.

example.text: Tax numbers and a bank account: easy to undo; now. Rent a house for a year: fairly easy; first, confirmed school places; February. Rent out our own house: fairly easy; first, a signed rental contract in Portugal; May. Lotte hands in her notice at her current job: hard; first, her new Portuguese income confirmed in a signed contract, and Ben's employer confirming in writing that his remote contract continues from Portugal; June. Buy a house: hardest; first, one full winter there and a green light on money; not before next year.

story.text: My own order was not the textbook one. I sold my house in Bali months before I had even visited Portugal, and moved out just before the trip. I spent two months travelling through Portugal, then went back to the Netherlands until the summer. That summer, I came back for a longer stay in an Airbnb close to the land, and signed the promissory contract about two months after my trip. About three months later, I signed the deed. That autumn and winter, I travelled between Portugal, the Netherlands and Bali: to be with my family, to start the paperwork, and to wrap up my life in Bali. The next spring, I came back for good. I stayed in the Airbnb again while I turned a shed into a small place to live. A contractor started renovating the ruin, and soon after, I moved onto the land. About eight months later, just before Christmas, we moved into the house. That speed came from the approved project, the right contractor, my experience, and being on site every day. Selling first worked for me because I had a reserve and had done this before. If this is your first move, I would take the easy-to-undo steps first.

tips: Build in extra time. Papers, contractors and sales often take longer than planned. My paperwork alone took about four months, and that was with help. Add a few months to every step you do not control yourself.

label: Part 4
title: Make your decision
promise: Go, not yet, or no. All three are real results.
intro: You have checked the five lights, looked at the difficult days and put the steps in order. Now you decide. Not forever: for now, with what you know.

Three rules help. Decide on paper first, then sleep on it for at least 48 hours before you tell anyone outside the decision. Decide together with the people it affects, after each of you has done your own thinking. And give every answer a date: when you start, when you review, or when you look at the question again.
talk: Tell the people close to you what you decided, and why. Not to ask for permission, but so they can support you, and so you hear your decision out loud.

finish.title: My Decision
finish.description: Go, not yet, or no, with your reasons, conditions and dates.

exercises.title: One last check: must-haves and dealbreakers
intro: In Step 1 you named what your new life needs and what you will not accept. Hold this option against them one last time. It is the cheapest red light there is: a broken dealbreaker ends this option, whatever the other lights say.

exercises.title: My Decision

fields.label: My decision question (from the Start)
My decision
Must-haves met, and no dealbreakers broken?
Why: my three main reasons
My lights: which are green, which are amber, and which are red
Conditions that must be true before the big steps
Who decided with me, and do we agree?
My first step
Date of my first step
When I will review this decision
What would make me change it

exercises.choice_explanations_intro: For "My decision", three answers are possible, and all three are good:
choice_explanations: Go. No light is red, and every amber light has a named condition, an action and a date. A go with conditions means you start preparing (Step 4, Prepare, is coming soon), but you take no hard-to-undo step until those conditions are met.

Not yet. The picture is right, but the conditions are not. Write down exactly what must change, and when you will look again. A "not yet" with a date is a decision. Without a date, it is a way of putting it off.
No. This option does not fit, or not at this price. That is a result, not a failure. Go back to Step 2 to look at another place, build the life you want where you are, or keep the life you have.

example.text: A completed page. Lotte and Ben are made up. The point is not their answer. It is that every line is filled in, including the conditions and the dates. Decision question: do we move to the Silver Coast with our two children, renting for a trial year from next summer? Decision: go, as a trial year, with conditions. We start preparing now; we sign nothing hard to undo until the conditions below are met. Must-haves: not all yet. All must-haves are met except one: a good school, which is an estimate until we have visited it and have places. That is a condition below. No dealbreakers broken. Why: our ordinary days there look like our Life Picture. The money lasts about 17 months even if everything costs 30% more, with our reserve and return fund untouched. The children are curious rather than against it. Lights: green: papers and place. Amber: money, until Lotte's income is confirmed; people, until care for Ben's mother is arranged; Plan B, until a tenant has signed for our house. Red: none. Conditions: Lotte's income confirmed. Care for Ben's mother arranged. A tenant signed for our house. School places confirmed. Who decided: both of us, after each of us filled in our own page. The children were heard. We agree. First step: meet two care providers for Ben's mother, before 15 March. Review: 1 April next year, whatever has happened by then. What would change it: no school places by May, or Lotte's income not confirmed by June: then we move the trial year back by one year.

story.text: Looking back, I did not decide in one moment. I decided in steps. The two-million question gave me the direction. Selling my house in Bali was the first big step, and I took it before I knew exactly where I would go. The campervan trip made the place real, and the third plot made the decision for me. For me, the biggest decision was not Portugal. It was choosing to start again. If you notice that you are waiting for certainty, remember that you will never have all of it. You need enough of it, and a plan for the rest.

exercises.title: If your answer is "not yet" or "no"
intro: A "not yet" or a "no" can feel like a step back. It is not. You now know more about what you want, and about what this option would require.

exercises.intro_after: Decided to build the life you want where you are? Go back to your Life Picture from Step 1, and choose one change for the next three months. Decided to keep the life you have? Write down what you want to protect, and why.
tips: A decision to wait is only a decision if it has a date. Put it in your calendar today.
